papers.title: A Growing Burden, a Persistent Gap: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome Education and Emergency Department Trends in Michigans Legal Cannabis Market
papers.abstract: Background: Since Michigan's legalization of recreational adult-use cannabis in December 2018, health care providers in the city of Kalamazoo, Michigan, have informally observed an increase in cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) presentations, although the extent of this increase has not been formally characterized locally. CHS is frequently underrecognized and misdiagnosed, often resulting in repeated emergency department (ED) visits and substantial diagnostic costs before a diagnosis is reached. Despite this clinical and financial burden, it is unclear whether consumers are adequately informed of this risk through point-of-sale or public health resources. Methods: A cross-sectional environmental scan was conducted to identify publicly available educational content about CHS on the websites of licensed cannabis retailers in Kalamazoo and relevant public health agencies. Provisioning centers and public health websites were screened using a structured coding rubric developed specifically for the environmental scan to assess the presence, depth, web page placement, and intended audience of CHS-related content. Additionally, the electronic medical records at a local teaching hospital in Kalamazoo were queried to identify ED visits with a primary diagnosis of CHS from January 1, 2010 to December 31, 2025. Results: Before the legalization of marijuana, the hospital recorded six ED encounters with the primary diagnosis of CHS between January 2010 and November 2018, and 274 ED encounters between December 2018 and December 2025 (mean age: 29 years; 157 females, 123 males). The incidence rate of CHS-related ED encounters was 57.2 times higher during the post-legalization period than during the pre-legalization period (95% CI, 26.0-157.3; exact Poisson rate-ratio test, p < 0.0001). Among the licensed Kalamazoo provisioning centers reviewed, only one mentioned CHS as a warning but did not describe symptoms or offer medical guidance. CHS content was not identified on the websites of the state or local health departments. Conclusion: Despite the growing clinical concern regarding CHS, consumer-facing educational resources remain scarce. Although this study cannot establish a causal relationship between the availability of CHS-related educational content and the observed increase in ED encounters following legalization, it identifies a substantial lack of CHS-specific warnings in the evaluated consumer-facing resources. Given the clinical and potential economic burden associated with delayed CHS recognition, we recommend that Michigans existing point-of-sale pamphlet requirement be amended to include CHS-specific warning language.

papers.title: Gendered patterns of reporting childhood abuse and quality of parental relationships across 21 nations: Descriptive findings from the Global Flourishing Study (GFS)
papers.abstract: Childhood experiences are important antecedents of adult flourishing, yet gender patterns in these experiences are under-studied in large global samples using a common survey instrument and population-based study design. From the Global Flourishing Study Wave 1 data (2022-2024), we analyzed responses from 203,430 adults (51% female, 49% male) in nationally representative samples from 21 nations on eight childhood-related items: experiencing physical or sexual abuse, feeling like an outsider in the family, feeling loved by one's mother or father, quality of relationship with one's mother or father, health growing up, and perceived family financial situation. Greater negative experiences were noted in more affluent nations (as measured by gross domestic product (GDP) per capita), with negative experiences generally reported more often among females than males, again especially in more affluent nations. Gender differences were more pronounced when it came to relationships with mothers compared to fathers. Perceptions regarding health and family finance while growing up did not show appreciable gender differences and had weaker correlations with other items.

papers.title: Hand-Washing Hygiene Knowledge, Attitude and Practice among University Students in the Post-COVID-19 Era: A Case of KCMC University, Moshi, Tanzania
papers.abstract: Background: Hand hygiene is a key public health intervention for preventing infectious diseases, including respiratory and gastrointestinal infections. Although the COVID-19 pandemic improved awareness and compliance, sustained adherence remains a challenge, with evidence showing a decline in practice after outbreaks, particularly among young adults in high-contact settings such as universities. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of handwashing hygiene among university students at KCMC University, Moshi, Tanzania, in the post-COVID-19 era. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 380 students at KCMC University. Data were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire, which captured information on socio-demographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding handwashing hygiene. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Associations between variables were assessed using logistic regression and multivariable analysis, and a p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: A total of 380 students participated in the study, with a mean age of 23.5 {+/-} 3.5 years. More than half 209 (55.0%) were aged 18-23 years, while 203 (53.4%) were female. Most participants had access to hand hygiene facilities 338 (88.9%). 338 (88.9%) participants had good knowledge of hand hygiene but attitudes were mostly negative 193 (50.8%), and practices were suboptimal, with 201 (52.9%) showing poor hand hygiene practices. Good hand hygiene knowledge was associated with access to hand hygiene facilities (AOR=2.84, 95% CI: 1.25-6.42, p=0.012) and formal training on hand hygiene (AOR=3.48, 95% CI: 1.24-9.76, p=0.018). Positive attitudes were associated with being in the fourth year or above (AOR=2.12, 95% CI: 1.16-3.89, p=0.015). Good hand hygiene practices were associated with access to hand hygiene facilities (AOR=2.67, 95% CI: 1.18-6.01, p=0.018) and formal training on hand hygiene (AOR=2.98, 95% CI: 1.19-7.48, p=0.020). Conclusion: Although knowledge and awareness of handwashing hygiene were generally high among university students, inconsistencies between knowledge and actual practices were observed in the post-COVID-19 era. Strengthening health education programs and ensuring continuous access to handwashing facilities may improve adherence to proper hand hygiene practices among university students.

papers.title: Prevalence and Multi-Domain Determinants of Elevated Blood Lead Levels Among Pregnant Women in Bangladesh: Evidence from the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey
papers.abstract: Background: Lead is a cumulative environmental toxicant for which no safe level of exposure has been identified, and pregnant women and their fetuses are particularly vulnerable because lead readily crosses the placenta and can be mobilised from maternal bone stores. Bangladesh conducted its first nationally representative blood lead testing among pregnant women through the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), but a detailed, multi-domain analysis of the determinants of elevated blood lead level (BLL) among this population has not yet been reported. Methods: We conducted a secondary cross-sectional analysis of 1,928 pregnant women aged 15-49 years with complete data from the women's dataset of Bangladesh MICS 2025. Elevated BLL was defined as [≥]5 g/dL. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to estimate unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for co-exposure to arsenic, cadmium and mercury and sociodemographic and socioeconomic covariates. Slope Index of Inequality (SII) as well as Relative Index of Inequality (RII) were used to quantify wealth-related inequality. Population attributable fractions (PAF) were estimated for three counterfactual scenarios, and adaptive least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used as a sensitivity analysis. Results: Elevated BLL was present among 6.2% of participants. In the adjusted model, a 2-fold rise in blood cadmium was associated with higher odds of elevated BLL (aOR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.21-1.96), whereas a 2-fold rise in blood mercury (aOR: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.48-0.83), rural residence (aOR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.32-0.94), secondary education (aOR: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.28-0.85) and post-secondary education (aOR: 0.22; 95% CI: 0.11-0.46) were associated with lower odds. Belonging to progressively wealthier quintiles was associated with markedly higher odds, BLL rising to an aOR of 10.32 (95% CI: 4.41-24.15) for the richest versus poorest quintile. The RII was 8.59 (95% CI: 4.24-17.40) and the SII was 0.159 (95% CI: 0.101-0.218), indicating a substantial pro-rich gradient in elevated BLL. Counterfactual scenarios suggested that shifting the population to secondary-level education could reduce the prevalence of elevated BLL by 52.9% (95% CI: 20.6-72.0) and shifting to rural residence by 24.3% (95% CI: 1.4-41.9). Adaptive LASSO variable selection produced estimates consistent in direction and magnitude with the fully adjusted model. Conclusion: In this national sample, approximately one out of every 16 pregnant women had blood lead levels that met or exceeded the action threshold set by the World Health Organization, with this issue being particularly prevalent among wealthier, urban, and less-educated women, and was compounded by co-exposure to cadmium. In Bangladesh, the typical pattern observed for maternal and child health indicators does not align with the inverse relationship found between household wealth and lead exposure. This suggests that the sources of exposure are not merely indicators of material poverty. Antenatal blood lead screening, source investigation, and equity-informed lead-reduction strategies that specifically reach wealthier and urban households are warranted.

papers.title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction
papers.abstract: Clinical foundation models learn patterns in longitudinal health records that can be reused across prediction tasks. However, the relative strengths of representation-based and generation-based prediction across clinical tasks remain unclear. Using longitudinal electronic health records from 3.77 million patients at a single hospital, we developed FERMAT (Foundation model for Exploring Real-world Multimodal health data using Autoregressive Trajectory modeling), a 65-million-parameter clinical foundation model. We compared predictions from task-specific predictors trained on patient representations with those derived from generated clinical event sequences. Representation-based prediction performed better in the disease-risk comparisons. In detailed analyses of five-year chronic kidney disease, fatty liver, and diabetes risk in a test cohort of 10,000 patients, representation-based predictors exceeded generation-based estimates by 0.098-0.115 in observation-weighted AUROC and had lower probability error. Generation-based prediction, in turn, performed better in predicting diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures recorded on the same day, a task motivated by the frequent presence of multiple events with the same date in hospital EHRs. Using 50 generated trajectories per patient, it achieved a Recall@10 of 71.0%, compared with 55.7% for representation-based prediction, with a paired improvement of 15.31 percentage points (95% CI, 13.92-16.79; n = 1,862). These findings demonstrate task-dependent strengths of representation-based and generation-based applications within a single clinical foundation model, providing an empirical basis for exploring how the two approaches can be used individually or combined to address clinical prediction needs.

papers.title: Sex differences in depression and substance use disorder diagnoses and overdose risk in British Columbia
papers.abstract: Background: Depression is a risk factor for overdose and is more commonly diagnosed among females. However, sex-differences in the association between depression, in isolation and in combination with substance use disorder (SUD), and overdose have not been examined at the population level in British Columbia (BC). This study described sex-and-age differences in associations between documented history of depression and/or SUD diagnoses and risk of fatal (FOD) and non-fatal overdose (NFOD). Methods: This study used linked administrative health data from the Provincial Health Services Authority Platform for Analytics and Data. The sample included BC residents aged 19-79 as of January 1st, 2015 (n=3,996,690). Exposures were classified as documented diagnosis history of 1) depression; 2) substance use disorder (SUD); 3) depression and SUD; and 4) neither condition, using physician billing and hospitalization records from 2010-2014. FOD (BC Coroners Service records) and NFOD (BC Emergency Health Services records) were ascertained from 2015 to 2024. Incidence rates per 10,000 person-years and unadjusted incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using Poisson regression, with neither diagnosis as reference, overall and stratified by sex and age. Results: There were 14,281 FOD (78.59% male) and 43,555 NFOD (69.45% male) cases. FOD incidence was higher among males overall; however, relative associations between diagnosis history and FOD risk were stronger among females. Depression diagnosis history was associated with a FOD IRR of 3.95 (CI: 3.56-4.38) among females and 2.46 (CI: 2.32-2.61) among males. IRRs for SUD and for depression and SUD were larger among females (108.07 [CI: 95.83-121.73] and 116.70 [CI: 106.51-127.96]) than males (26.69 [CI: 25.57-28.18] and 31.21 [CI: 29.81-32.67]). NFOD findings were similar but attenuated (depression IRR: 3.22 [CI: 3.08-3.38]) in females; 2.29 [CI: 2.21-2.37] in males). Conclusion: A documented history of depression and/or SUD was more strongly associated with FOD and NFOD risk among females, despite higher incidence overall among males. Future research should consider the potential role of other sociodemographic factors in explaining sex differences in associations between diagnosis history and overdose risk.

papers.title: Association of childhood experiences with wellbeing and flourishing outcomes in Indian adults: Evidence from the India Sample of the Global Flourishing Study (GFS)
papers.abstract: Background: Childhood experiences contribute to health and wellbeing across the life course, yet research from low- and middle-income countries has largely focused on a few outcomes rather than broader patterns of adult wellbeing, behaviors, and social and financial circumstances. Methods: In this cross-sectional analysis, we used a nationally representative sample of adults in India (N = 12,765; aged [≥] 18 years) from the Global Flourishing Study (GFS) Wave 1 (2023) to examine associations between eight retrospectively reported childhood experience items, 45 adult outcomes, and two composite flourishing indices. Survey-weighted linear, logistic, and proportional-odds models adjusted for age, gender, education, and residential setting, with Bonferroni correction were used to assess associations and effect modification by gender. Findings: Although the breadth and strength of associations differed across childhood experiences, less favorable childhood experiences were generally associated with poorer wellbeing and flourishing, greater odds of adverse health outcomes, and reduced access to resources and safety in adult life. However, outcomes related to prosocial behaviors showed a different pattern: childhood abuse (physical or sexual) was associated with greater odds of volunteering (OR 1.31, 95% confidence interval or CI [1.13,1.51]), feeling like an outsider in one's family with greater odds of donating (OR 1.80, 95% CI [1.52,2.13]), volunteering (OR 1.53, 95% CI [1.28,1.82]), and helping a stranger (OR 1.49, 95% CI [1.27,1.74]). Associations were broadly similar between females and males, with little evidence of gender differences. Interpretation: Associations of childhood adversity with poorer health and increased prosocial behavior in adult life may reflect unmeasured social, cultural, or dispositional factors and heterogeneous life-course responses. Nevertheless, these findings support strengthening child-protection, financial assistance programs, and mental health services in India.

papers.title: Prevalence of suicidal ideation and its associated factors among school-going adolescents in northern Bangladesh: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Adolescent suicidal ideation is a critical public health issue, yet empirical evidence on its prevalence and associated factors among adolescents in northern Bangladesh remains limited. This study estimated the 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation and examined its associated factors among school-going adolescents in Nilphamari District, Bangladesh. A cross-sectional survey was conducted between May and June 2026 among 365 adolescents aged 13-19 years across eight secondary schools and colleges. Self-administered questionnaires assessed suicidal ideation alongside validated tools for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and perceived social support (MSPSS). Factors associated with suicidal ideation were examined using multivariable logistic regression. The 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation was 30.7% (112/365; 95% CI 26.0%-35.7%). In the primary multivariable model, moderate depression (AOR = 6.05, 95% CI 1.03-35.38; p = 0.046) and moderately severe depression (AOR = 6.86, 95% CI 1.05-44.62; p = 0.044) were associated with higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to minimal depression. However, this association was not statistically significant in a sensitivity analysis using the PHQ-8 score after excluding Item 9 (AOR = 1.06, 95% CI: 0.96-1.17; p = 0.228). Loneliness "often" showed the strongest association with suicidal ideation (AOR = 10.59, 95% CI: 2.53-44.35; p = 0.001). Suicidal ideation was also associated with truancy of 6-9 days (AOR 4.44, 95% CI 1.24-15.90; p = 0.022), truancy of [≥]10 days (AOR 3.77, 95% CI 1.34-10.59; p = 0.012), intentional self-harm (AOR = 2.51, 95% CI: 1.17-5.41; p = 0.018), and physical harm exposure (AOR = 2.63, 95% CI: 1.24-5.57; p = 0.012). Maternal secondary education was associated with lower odds of suicidal ideation (AOR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.12-0.99; p = 0.048). Suicidal ideation was common among school-going adolescents in northern Bangladesh, affecting nearly one in three participants. Early school-based identification and support for adolescents experiencing mental-health and psychosocial difficulties, together with family engagement and strengthened suicide-prevention services, are warranted.

papers.title: Laboratory Evaluation of Cyclospora cayetanensis in Wastewater: Expanding Pathogen Targets for Regulatory Public Health Surveillance
papers.abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has become a cornerstone of public health surveillance, yet routine regulatory monitoring remains largely focused on respiratory viruses and selecting antimicrobial resistant bacteria. Emerging foodborne parasites, such as Cyclospora cayetanensis, remain excluded from standard environmental surveillance panels despite increasing domestic outbreaks. This study presents a laboratory-based pilot protocol evaluating the feasibility of extracting and quantifying C. cayetanensis from urban wastewater across the Chicago metropolitan area. Using sample concentration via centrifugation and mechanical bead-beating, automated magnetic bead nucleic acid extraction, and digital PCR (dPCR), we demonstrate high-sensitivity detection in municipal influents and sewer nodes. These findings establish a proof-of-concept laboratory methodology to support the expansion of regulatory public health surveillance frameworks to include non-routine protozoan pathogens.

papers.title: Daylight Saving Time, Acute Sleep Disruption, and Return-to-Baseline Patterns in All of Us Fitbit Data
papers.abstract: Seasonal daylight saving time (DST) transitions abruptly alter the alignment between clock time, environmental light, and sleep. In preregistered analyses, we used longitudinal Fitbit data from the All of Us Research Program to compare sleep around 13 seasonal transitions in Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah with sleep on the same dates in Arizona, where clocks do not change. The sample included 1,522 participants and 6,658 participant-transition windows. Following the spring transition, sleep duration changed more from one night to the next in Mountain states than in Arizona (14.6 minutes, 95% CI [7.2, 22.0]), even though sleep duration itself on day +1 showed little evidence of a DST-related reduction (-8.4 minutes, 95% CI [-17.3, 0.6]). Sleep timing shifted later after the spring transition and about 28 minutes earlier after the fall transition. Among Mountain-state observations with a large post-transition departure from usual sleep duration, the median return to the usual range was two nights. Nearly the same two-night pattern appeared in Arizona after similarly large sleep departures, indicating that this return pattern was not specific to DST. Greater baseline sleep-duration variability predicted a greater likelihood of remaining outside the usual range at days +7 and +14. Seasonal clock changes produced acute sleep disruption, while the Arizona comparison shows that a rapid return to baseline should not be interpreted as the duration of recovery from DST itself.

papers.title: Socioeconomic determinants of elevated blood lead among children aged 12-59 months in Bangladesh: a nationally representative survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundChildhood lead exposure is a major global health concern. The 2025 Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) measured blood lead in a nationally representative sample of children aged 12-59 months for the first time. Preliminary reports suggested elevated blood lead was more common in wealthier urban households, contrary to the usual assumption. MethodsWe analysed 10,622 children with a valid blood lead result (10,458 with complete covariate data for regression models). Elevated blood lead was defined as [≥] 5 {micro}g/dL. Prevalences are survey-weighted with design-based confidence intervals. Associations were estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression using stratified-cluster (Taylor-linearised) variance, and checked with a stratified bootstrap of primary sampling units and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control. Sensitivity analyses varied the outcome definition, the sample, and the weighting. ResultsSurvey-weighted prevalence of elevated blood lead was 38.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 37.2-39.9%). Prevalence rose monotonically from 30.2% in the poorest to 51.9% in the richest wealth quintile. In the fully adjusted model, each wealth quintile was associated with 23% higher odds (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.23, 95% CI 1.16-1.30), each level of maternal education with 20% lower odds (AOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76-0.84), and urban residence with 37% higher odds (AOR 1.37, 95% CI 1.18-1.59). Household crowding was associated with higher odds (AOR 1.16 per person per room, 95% CI 1.10-1.24). The wealth-education interaction had AOR 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.98). In an exploratory contrast, weighted prevalence was 76.2% among children in the richest quintile with mothers having at most primary education versus 19.5% among those in the poorest quintile with mothers having higher secondary or tertiary education (prevalence ratio 3.9, 95% CI 2.6-6.0). Adjusted odds relative to Barishal ranged from 0.39 in Rajshahi to 3.29 in Dhaka. ConclusionsIn this cross-sectional survey, elevated blood lead was more prevalent among wealthier and urban households and among children of less educated mothers, with large geographic variation. Lead prevention and source-identification efforts should therefore not be restricted to poor communities; prevalence remained high even in the poorest quintile. Interpretation is limited by substantial missing blood lead results and coding uncertainty.

papers.title: Longitudinal Associations between the Built Environment, Biological Aging and Cognition
papers.abstract: Features of urbanicity have been linked to poor psychiatric health in adulthood, but little is known about their relationship with biological age and cognition earlier in life. Using the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), we tested associations between the built environment and epigenetic ages (EpiAgeAltum, EpiAgeHorvath, EpiAgePACE) (n=2,452), brain age (n=751), and cognition (n=12,199). Analyses were replicated in Generation R and triangulated in the Millennium Cohort Study. The built environment was not associated with epigenetic ages ({beta}Altum range = 0.013-0.015, p range = .466-.689; {beta}Horvath range = -0.011-0.023, p range = .182-.728; {beta}PACE range = -0.045-0.013, p range = .131-.524) or brain age ({beta} range = 0.022-0.028, p range = .337-.429). A negative association with cognition was observed in Generation R. We provide no consistent evidence that childhood built environment exposure relates to biological age and cognition in adolescence, suggesting these relationships may emerge in later life.

papers.title: Probabilistic forecasting of prefecture-level influenza in Japan accounting for surveillance data release histories
papers.abstract: BackgroundPublic-health use of influenza surveillance - situational awareness, planning for clinical surge, and issuing advisories or warnings - needs more than an accurate point estimate of next weeks count. What matters operationally is whether a rise is caught early, whether the direction of change is right, and whether an alert threshold is about to be crossed, all with honest uncertainty. For such use a forecast must also respect reporting delay, later data revision, and the calibration of its prediction intervals. Using Japans sentinel surveillance, we evaluated short-term probabilistic forecasts that respect the data release history, and we measured what adding other surveillance series contributes, focusing on the properties that matter for public-health decisions. MethodsThe target was the number of influenza reports per sentinel site in each of the 47 prefectures. For each forecast we predicted, as quantiles, the value 1-4 weeks after the most recent observed week. We compared three models: a ridge regression trained jointly across prefectures; a gradient-boosting quantile regression (GBQR) that learns from many surveillance series; and their equal-weight combination on the log scale. Six seasons were used to develop the models. The 2025/26 season was held out as a temporal evaluation period after the specification was fixed; because its epidemic profile had already been seen, it is not a fully independent prospective test. We scored forecasts with the weighted interval score (WIS) and checked prediction-interval coverage. For the Japanese target series we used the value first published for each week; some auxiliary series were taken as retrieved and therefore include later revisions. ResultsIn 2025/26, the combinations WIS relative to a persistence forecast was 0.841, 0.811, 0.794 and 0.818 at horizons of 1-4 observed weeks - that is, 16-21% lower than persistence. Coverage of the 80% prediction interval was 79.7%, 77.1%, 74.5% and 75.1%, and of the 95% interval 94.3%, 93.4%, 92.6% and 91.8%. Adding auxiliary series improved the GBQR over the development period. However, on the original scale the combinations edge over ridge regression was not statistically clear, and in some low-level rising phases the combination did worse than ridge. ConclusionsOver the period studied, models that share information across regions scored better than a persistence forecast. For public-health use, however, the operative questions are the real lead time once reporting delay is accounted for, whether rises from low levels and threshold exceedances are caught in time, and whether the upper prediction intervals are wide enough; on these, the present evidence is not yet sufficient. The 2025 change to the sentinel system also means that pre-change advisory and warning thresholds cannot be read mechanically. A prospective evaluation with strictly controlled data availability is needed before such forecasts are used to support advisories or planning.

papers.title: Does active travel behaviour moderate the association between the built environment and depression?
papers.abstract: BackgroundBuilt environment characteristics have been associated with depressive symptoms, whilst active travel behaviour is linked to improved mental health. However, it remains unclear whether active travel buffers associations between increased exposure to the built environment and worse mental health. MethodsIn this pre-registered study, participants were 10,310 mothers (mean age = 28.11, SD = 4.83) participating in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC). A latent built environment factor was measured at study enrolment, active travel behaviour at a 2-year follow-up, and depressive symptoms at a 4-year follow-up. Moderation was examined using adjusted linear regression models including an interaction term between the built environment factor and active travel behaviour. ResultsThe built environment factor was positively associated with depressive symptoms ({beta} = 0.023, p = .012). Active travel behaviour was not associated with depressive symptoms ({beta} = -0.002, p = .854) and did not moderate the association between the built environment factor and depressive symptoms ({beta} = -0.002, p = .865), after adjusting for covariates, including age, familial depressive history, socioeconomic risk factors, physical activity, baseline depressive symptoms and smoking. ConclusionContrary to expectations, active travel behaviour does not modify associations between the built environment and depressive symptoms. These findings provide no evidence that active travel mitigates mental health risks associated with the built environment in this population. What is already known on this topicO_LISome features of the built environment have been associated with poor mental health, and active travel has been linked to better psychological wellbeing. However, it is unclear whether active travel can reduce the mental health risks associated with more urbanised environments. C_LI What this study addsO_LIWe tested active travel as a potential modifier of the longitudinal association between the built environment and depressive symptoms. C_LIO_LIWe found no evidence that active travel buffered this association in a sample of mothers. C_LI How this study might affect research, practice or policyO_LIEngagement in active travel alone may be insufficient to offset mental health risks associated with the built environment, and future research should test whether these relationships differ across populations, travel purposes and levels of active travel. C_LI

papers.title: Impact of conditional mobile data credits on caregivers use of an early childhood digital health intervention: a nested cluster-randomized controlled trial in Andean Peru
papers.abstract: As internet and mobile phone access increases, digital health interventions are increasingly used to support remote and low-resource populations. In many settings, the health impact of digital interventions is constrained by limited or short-lived engagement. We tested if conditional mobile data credit incentives increase digital intervention engagement within a digital intervention trial. This nested cluster randomized controlled trial was conducted with caregivers of children 3-9 months at baseline. Of 72 neighborhood clusters from the treatment arm of the parent trial (evaluating a digital early childhood development intervention), 20 were randomly assigned to treatment and 52 as controls. Eligible participants had a phone provider through which mobile data credits could be most affordably administered. Treated participants received around 250 MB mobile data credits every two weeks, conditional upon using the digital intervention at least once in the same period. Credits were digitally administered via a third-party service. Digital intervention engagement (primary outcome) was monitored continuously until endline data collection approximately 2 years after assignment. Secondary outcomes included caregivers views, behaviors, and early childhood development. We used intent-to-treat analyses to assess all outcomes. This trial was registered as NCT05202106 at clinicaltrials.gov and was completed in 2025. Participants were recruited between September 2021 and March 2023 (N Treatment = 147; N Control = 333). Conditional mobile data credits extended engagement with the digital early childhood development intervention by 6.50 weeks on average (treatment mean = 26.19 weeks, control mean = 19.69; p=0.011). No significant impacts were identified on secondary outcomes. As such, mobile data credits may be a cost-effective way for increasing caregiver engagement with digital health intervention in low resource settings.

papers.title: The Long Road to Care: A Mixed Methods Analysis of Referral Delays for Pediatric Injury Patients in Northern Tanzania
papers.abstract: Every day, 1900 children die from an injury, with the majority in low-and middle-income countries. In Tanzania, reaching definitive care, or the appropriate final level of care for a childs injury, often requires referral to a higher level facility. This hierarchical system introduces challenges that may lead to delayed care and, for severely injured children, cause mortality. The aim was to identify patient, healthcare provider, and health system-level barriers to timely referral for pediatric injury patients at the first site of care in order to identify targets for an intervention to reduce time to definitive care. In this mixed-methods study, a pediatric injury registry was established at three health facilities spanning three health system levels in Northern Tanzania. Thirty family caregivers of pediatric injury patients participated in interviews, while healthcare providers participated in four focus group discussions. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research framed interview guides and thematic analysis of the qualitative data. Of 782 patients enrolled in the pediatric injury registry from Aug 2024-Aug 2025, 269 were referred. Most visited 1-4 facilities before reaching definitive care (range 1-6). The median time from injury to definitive care was 15.1 hours (IQR 1.8-33). Qualitative data collection with family caregivers and healthcare providers revealed barriers to explain the delays to care in the outer setting (such as non-standardized referral pathways), the inner setting (such as delays in the decision to refer), and individual characteristics (such as inadequate training in pediatric injury care). According to the World Health Organization standards, every child who needs referral should be sent within 2 hours of arrival. To improve the referral delays found in this study, a locally co-designed, multicomponent health systems intervention for healthcare providers at the first site of care must be developed that includes pediatric injury care training and standardized referral decision support. Key MessagesO_LIInjuries are important contributors to child morbidity and mortality globally, with low-and middle-income settings like Tanzania disproportionately affected. C_LIO_LIIn Tanzania there is a complex health system where pediatric injury patients present to primary health facilities first, and are referred up the health system until they reach the definitive care that they need. C_LIO_LIBarriers at the outer setting, inner setting, and individual level of the health system contribute to delays in reaching definitive care. C_LIO_LIIn order to combat these delays and improve child morbidity and mortality, a locally co-designed, multicomponent health systems intervention at the level of the first site of care must be developed that includes standardized referral decision processes. C_LI

papers.title: Physicians' Industrial Action: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis Assessing Impact in 11 Kenyan Neonatal Units
papers.abstract: Background. Skilled healthcare workers are essential for neonatal survival; however, the Kenyan public health system has historically faced strikes compounded by a human resource crisis. Evidence on how strikes affect neonatal care and mortality remains limited. This study evaluated changes in neonatal admissions, clinical care processes, and inpatient mortality associated with 56 days of disruption during the 2024 Kenyan physicians' strike. Methods. We conducted a retrospective interrupted time-series analysis of 12,184 admissions to 11 Kenyan neonatal units implementing with the NEST360 Alliance, recorded in the Neonatal Inpatient Dataset from December 2023 to August 2024. Weekly admissions and inpatient mortality were modeled over a 72-week window (27,638 admissions) using hospital-clustered generalized estimating equations with seasonal terms. Care processes, case fatality, and birthweight-specific mortality were compared across study periods. Results. Weekly admissions fell from 413 to 189 during the strike (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 0.49, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.31-0.75), approximately 1,700 fewer admissions than expected, and returned to baseline afterward (IRR 1.00, CI 0.81-1.23). Newborns admitted during the strike were of lower birthweight, more often premature, and more often outborn. Admissions fell across all birth-location categories, most steeply among inborn neonates. No measurable change was detected in documented inpatient coverage of care measures, in crude mortality (12.5% to 14.9%; risk ratio (RR) 1.07, CI 0.85-1.33), or in trend-adjusted mortality (IRR 0.88, CI 0.53-1.45). Case fatality among neonates with recorded infection doubled, from 4.7% to 9.6% (RR 2.06, CI 1.18-3.58; adjusted p = 0.047). Conclusions. The 2024 physicians' strike was associated with severe disruption to neonatal service utilization, with admissions returning to baseline when the strike ended. Among newborns who continued to reach care, inpatient mortality did not change measurably, but case fatality among those with recorded infection doubled. This analysis was confined to inpatient data; hence, the outcomes of newborns who did not reach the hospitals were not captured. Both inpatient and population-level data are needed to assess the full impact of the strike. Mitigating harm during future labor disruptions requires interventions such as resilient care models, formalized task-shifting protocols, and minimum service coverage agreements.

papers.title: Hand hygiene knowledge and practices among health care workers in Uganda: Evidence from Mukono and Kagadi districts
papers.abstract: BackgroundHand hygiene (HH) is one of the most effective measures to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and limit the transmission of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens in healthcare facilities (HCFs). Effective HH programs depend not only on the availability of essential resources but also on healthcare workers (HCWs) knowledge, attitudes, and adherence to recommended HH practices. Despite the critical role of these factors in improving infection prevention and control (IPC), evidence on HH knowledge and practices among HCWs remains limited. In Uganda, such evidence from lower-level district health facilities is particularly scarce. This study assessed HH knowledge and practices, along with associated factors, among HCWs at selected health facilities in the Mukono and Kagadi districts of Uganda. MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 586 HCWs at selected health facilities in the Mukono and Kagadi districts from May to June 2025. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered via KoboCollect, covering participants socio-demographic and professional characteristics, HH knowledge, self-reported HH practices, and facility-related factors. Descriptive statistics summarized the data, and modified Poisson regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE), accounting for clustering of HCWs within facilities, was used to estimate prevalence ratios for factors associated with HH knowledge and practices. ResultsOverall, 82.1% of HCWs had adequate HH knowledge, and 43.0% had good HH practice. Nearly all respondents correctly identified the recommended handwashing duration (98.8%), the minimum effective alcohol concentration for alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) (98.8%), proper HH as the most effective method for preventing HAIs (97.6%), and 89.9% correctly listed all five WHO Moments for HH. HCWs in Mukono were more likely to have adequate HH knowledge than those in Kagadi (aPR = 1.36; 95% CI: 1.15-1.60). HCWs with 6-10 years of experience had higher knowledge of HH than those with less than two years of experience (aPR=1.16, 95% CI: 1.02-1.33). Good HH practice was significantly more common among clinical officers (aPR=1.36, 95% CI: 1.06-1.75) and other cadres (aPR=1.65, 95% CI: 1.14-2.39) than nurses and nursing assistants. ConclusionHCWs demonstrated high HH knowledge but suboptimal HH practice, suggesting a gap between knowledge and self-reported practice. Interventions should move beyond knowledge dissemination to strengthen compliance through multimodal, cadre-specific strategies, particularly for nurses and nursing assistants.

papers.title: Developing a social vulnerability index from real-world electronic health records using natural language processing
papers.abstract: BackgroundSocial vulnerability is associated with adverse health outcomes, but existing social vulnerability indices often rely on cohort-based and self-reported data, potentially limiting their population-level applicability. Therefore, this study aimed to develop an SVI from routinely collected electronic health records (EHRs) using natural language processing (NLP) and examine its association with mortality and healthcare utilization. MethodEHR data from 193,629 individuals aged 35-102 from the Wellbeing Services County of Central Finland between years 2010 and 2023 were used in this study. A 6-item SVI (total score 0-6) was developed from free-text clinical notes using deep-learning-based NLP. SVI scores were calculated at baseline and annually for individuals. Associations between baseline SVI and all-cause mortality and healthcare utilization were assessed over 12-year follow-up using Cox and count models. ResultsThe mean baseline SVI among all participants was 0.35 (range 0-6). Women had higher SVI (0.39) than men (0.32, p<0.001). SVI increased with age. One unit increase in SVI was associated with a higher risk of mortality (Hazard Ratio (HR) 1.23; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) (1.21-1.24), a higher odds of using healthcare services (Odds Ratio (OR) = 1.20; 95% CI): 1.19-1.21) and a greater healthcare service use (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) = 1.07; 95% CI: 1.06-1.07). DiscussionAn index capturing multiple domains of social vulnerability can be derived from EHRs using NLP. Higher SVI was associated with increased mortality and healthcare utilization. These findings support the potential of EHR data for assessing social vulnerability and related health risks. HighlightsO_LISVI can be derived from free-text EHR data using NLP in an unselected population. C_LIO_LIHigher EHR-derived social vulnerability was associated with mortality and healthcare use. C_LIO_LIEHR data may help identify individuals needing targeted assessment or support C_LI

papers.title: Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Among Herbal Practitioners: A Mixed-Methods Study of Reporting Practices, Associated Factors, and Pharmacovigilance System Barriers in the Greater Accra Region, Ghana
papers.abstract: BackgroundHerbal medicinal products are widely used in Ghana; however, adverse drug reaction (ADR) reporting associated with these products remains limited, posing challenges to pharmacovigilance and medicine safety surveillance. This study assessed trends in herbal medicine-related ADR reporting, determined the prevalence and factors associated with ADR reporting among herbal practitioners, and explored barriers to ADR reporting in Ghana. MethodsA mixed-methods study involving secondary pharmacovigilance data review, an analytic cross-sectional survey, and qualitative in-depth interviews was conducted. Secondary data on herbal medicine-related ADR reports submitted to the Ghana Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) between 2014 and 2024 were reviewed descriptively. The cross-sectional survey involved 271 herbal practitioners selected through multi-stage probability sampling across seven districts in the Greater Accra Region. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and logistic regression in IBM SPSS Statistics version 26. The qualitative component involved 15 purposively selected participants, and thematic analysis was conducted using MAXQDA 2020. ResultsA total of 117 herbal medicine-related ADR reports met the inclusion criteria and were analysed from the Ghana FDA pharmacovigilance database between 2014 and 2024. Among 271 surveyed herbal practitioners, 11.8% (95% CI: 8.0-15.6) reported submitting at least one ADR report during the preceding 12 months. In multivariable analysis, lack of ADR reporting forms or job aids (aOR = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.04-0.31) and lack of exposure to Ghana FDA ADR reporting guidelines (aOR = 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.32) were independently associated with lower odds of ADR reporting. Qualitative findings identified causal uncertainty, inadequate training, weak reporting systems, commercial interests, and limited regulatory support as major barriers to reporting. ConclusionADR reporting associated with herbal medicinal products was limited within the national pharmacovigilance system and among surveyed herbal practitioners. System-level barriers, particularly limited access to reporting tools and FDA reporting guidance, were associated with lower reporting. Strengthening pharmacovigilance infrastructure, improving practitioner training, and increasing access to reporting tools may improve herbal medicine safety surveillance.

papers.title: Targeted Deployment of Long-Acting HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis in sub-Saharan Africa: Modelled Impact on Infections and Programme Costs to 2050
papers.abstract: BackgroundLong-acting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (LAP) could transform HIV prevention in sub-Saharan Africa, but its public-health impact and value-for-money will depend on whether programmes can reach people at greatest risk. We quantified the potential impact and efficiency of targeted LAP deployment across sub-Saharan Africa. MethodsWe developed a deterministic, age-structured compartmental model of HIV among adults aged 15 years or older in African countries accounting for 98% of adults living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) was assumed to reach 95% coverage by 2030 in all countries. LAP was assumed to reduce HIV acquisition by 96%. In model analyses, LAP was allocated according to rules that specify the degree to which programmes can effectively allocate it to those at greatest risk of acquiring HIV, including using a persons district, sex and age-group, and other signals of risk. FindingsAcross 34 countries, allocating a fixed quantity of LAP by district, sex and age averted 2 - 21 times as many infections as uniform allocation; perfect identification of within-group risk, an upper bound, raised this to 5 - 32 times. Multipliers were largest in low-prevalence countries, where absolute impact was smallest; in higher burden settings, they were 2 - 6 and 5 - 11, respectively. If 3 million people used LAP from 2028 in the 11 countries currently receiving Global Fund-supported lenacapavir, uniform allocation would avert about 41,000 infections by 2050, targeting by district, sex and age about 601,000 (range 360,000 - 1,660,000), and perfect risk targeting about 972,000 (490,000 - 3,570,000). Discounted averted ART costs fully offset LAP costs by 2050 at a total cost of up to [~]US$50 per person-year with perfect risk targeting, $30 with targeting by district, sex and age, and $2 with uniform allocation. Expansion to 15 million users by 2035 brought modelled adult incidence across sub-Saharan Africa below 0.1 per 1000 person-years in 2049, about a decade earlier than projected without LAP, under the assumption that ART coverage reaches 95% in every country by 2030. InterpretationTargeting determines both the impact and the net cost of LAP. Allocation by district, sex and age is feasible now and multiplies the infections averted by each person-year of LAP. LAP offsets its cost through averted treatment only when it is targeted and its fully loaded cost is near the low end of current estimates. Better identification of people at highest risk within demographic groups, and sustained use among them, could add substantially to impact. The same approach could guide the allocation of LAP in other settings where HIV risk is concentrated.

papers.title: Use of routine clinical data in adults with chronic diseases for identifying risk of frailty: results from the UK Biobank study
papers.abstract: Frailty assessment is increasingly recommended for risk stratification in chronic disease management, but systematic clinical screening for frailty remains difficult to implement because it is resource-intensive. We investigated whether routinely collected clinical measures could be repurposed to prioritize adults with chronic diseases for clinical frailty assessment. We conducted a prediction study using UK Biobank data. A stacked ensemble model was developed using 12 routinely and low cost measured clinical variables to predict frailty. Gain metrics were used to quantify the proportion of frailty cases identified when screening was restricted to individuals with the highest predicted risk of frailty. We compared health profiles (mortality, polypharmacy, self-rated health, falls) of frail and non-frail individuals across different levels of predicted risk. The robustness of this screening strategy was evaluated across 3,284 modelling settings. Among 281,729 participants (mean age 57{middle dot}9; 54{middle dot}7% women) with at least one chronic condition, 5{middle dot}8% were frail. In the validation sample (N validation=93,910, N training=187,819), screening only the 20% of participants with the highest predicted risk of frailty identified 55{middle dot}6% of all frailty cases, corresponding to a 2{middle dot}78-fold improvement compared to random screening. Overall, the model recovered 53{middle dot}4% of the maximum achievable improvement over random screening. Frailty remained always associated with poor outcomes. Screening performance remained consistent across alternative modelling settings. Routinely collected clinical measures can improve the efficiency of frailty screening among adults living with chronic diseases by prioritizing individuals based on their level of risk. Since these data are already gathered during routine care, this risk-prioritization strategy could support scalable screening without increasing testing burden or clinical workload.

papers.title: Taught but not retained: disaster medicine in the education of seven health professions in Germany-a nationwide cross-sectional survey of 8,133 students and trainees
papers.abstract: BackgroundDisaster medicine has been a formal curricular recommendation in German health professions education since 2006, and comparable recommendations exist internationally. Evidence on implementation is confined almost entirely to human medicine, rests on faculty self-reports or small student samples, and measures delivery rather than retention. Whether curricular exposure is associated with willingness to serve has not been adequately examined in interprofessional samples. ObjectiveWe aimed to characterize disaster medicine education across 7 health professions in Germany, distinguishing delivery from retention, to identify profession-specific gaps and training priorities, and to examine how educational and experiential factors relate to willingness to serve. MethodsWe conducted an anonymous nationwide online cross-sectional survey of students and trainees across 7 health professions in Germany between July 9 and August 25, 2026, recruited through institutional distribution lists. The interprofessionally developed instrument comprised 48 items. We assessed delivery and retention of 12 disaster medicine topics (4-point scale), self-rated confidence in 22 clinical and nursing skills (6-point scale), desired content, formats, motivators and barriers, and formal and spontaneous willingness. For all rating scales, higher values denote the more favorable level. We derived a delivery-retention gap and a want-deficit index, examined the dimensional structure of the competence battery, tested for differential item functioning by prior civil protection engagement, and modeled willingness with a cumulative link model. ResultsOf 8133 respondents (completion rate 87.5%), 33.1% had never been taught disaster medicine and 25.0% only in passing; 22.1% had comprehensive teaching including practical exercises. Across the 12 topics, the proportion able to retrieve content confidently never exceeded 23.9%; the delivery-retention gap reached 47.3 percentage points. More than half (54.6%) had never taken part in a practical exercise. Competence formed more than 1 dimension: 18 acute-technical items loaded 0.54-0.86 on the first factor, 4 relational and nursing items 0.14-0.28. Prior civil protection engagement was associated with higher confidence on every acute-technical item (Cliff delta 0.26-0.55) and lower confidence on all 4 relational items (-0.22 to -0.09). Willingness was high and homogeneous across groups (78.7% formal, 84.1% spontaneous), whereas competence varied by about 2 scale points. Adjusted, active civil protection engagement (odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 2.12-2.94) and practical exercise experience (odds ratio 1.78, 95% CI 1.54-2.05) were the strongest predictors; curricular exposure contributed weakly (odds ratio 1.06 per SD, 95% CI 0.99-1.14). ConclusionsTwo decades after the curricular recommendation, disaster medicine is largely absent from health professions education in Germany, and what is delivered is not retained. Willingness is nevertheless high and largely decoupled from competence, so qualification and recruitment require separate instruments. Curricula should be prioritized by the coincidence of demand and deficit rather than by coverage, built for retention, and should treat relational and nursing competence as a distinct learning objective.

papers.title: Climate factors and child health in Sweden: a nationwide whole-population study of 4.6 million school-aged children
papers.abstract: BackgroundShort-term weather conditions can trigger paediatric hospital admissions, but evidence remains limited on the health relevance of intraday temperature variability, humidity, and precipitation, and generally on which subgroups are most susceptible. MethodsWe conducted a nationwide case time-series study of Swedish children and adolescents aged 6-18 years using linked register data. Associations between daily mean temperature, intraday temperature variability, relative humidity, and precipitation and inpatient hospitalisations were estimated with Poisson regression (individual fixed effects) combined with distributed lag non-linear models over lags 0-21 days. Outcomes included all-cause hospitalisation and cause-specific admissions. Effect modification was examined by sex, age group, socioeconomic indicators, region, and calendar periods. FindingsAmong 4,638,247 children and adolescents in the cohort, 1,070,702 (23.1%) experienced at least one inpatient hospitalisation, contributing 1,736,169 hospitalisation events. All-cause hospitalisation increased with higher mean temperature, with risk highest at hot extremes. Intraday temperature variability showed a U-shaped association, with higher rates at both lowest and highest exposure levels. Relative humidity showed no association with hospitalisation risk. Higher precipitation was associated with increased hospitalisation risk, but estimates at high rainfall levels were imprecise. Stratified analyses indicated modest differences by sex and socioeconomic indicators, but clearer heterogeneity by age and region, with the highest risks among younger children and in East Sweden; associations varied across calendar periods and were imprecise for most cause-specific outcomes. Sensitivity analyses mostly showed that the main curve shapes were robust. InterpretationShort-term exposure to hot temperatures, both low and high intraday temperature variability, and higher levels of precipitation were associated with an increased risk of all-cause hospitalisation among children in Sweden, with clearer variation by age group and region than by sex or socioeconomic position. These findings support targeting paediatric climate-health preparedness and early-warning systems toward younger children and higher-risk regions such as eastern Sweden and extending such systems beyond mean temperature to include intraday temperature variability, a distinct, currently overlooked driver of risk that heat-focused systems are not designed to capture. FundingsThis research was funded by Formas, the Swedish Research Council for Sustainable Development (grant no. 2023-01774 and 2022-01845) and the Swedish Research Council (2025-02804 and 2022-06599). Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe identified epidemiological studies examining climatic exposures and hospitalisation among children, published in any language up to June 26, 2026, in MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science. Search terms combined paediatric populations and hospital admissions with climate exposures and DLNM (e.g., (child OR paediatric*) AND (hospital* OR admission*) AND (temperature OR heat OR cold OR "diurnal temperature range" OR "temperature variability" OR intraday AND humidity OR precipitation OR rainfall) AND (DLNM OR "distributed lag" OR case-time series* OR case-crossover*) (n = 2526). Previous studies have reported associations between ambient temperatures and increased risk of paediatric morbidity, particularly for respiratory and infectious diseases. However, evidence is often limited to smaller exposed groups, single healthcare settings or geographic areas, cause specific outcomes, aggregated data, and incomplete assessment of lagged effects and subgroup vulnerability. Analyses of different climatic exposures, such as temperature, humidity, and precipitation, remain rare. Added value of this studyOur study used linked whole-population register data from more than 4.6 million school-aged children and adolescents aged 6-18 years in Sweden. This is one of the largest whole-population cohort studies of individual-level climate-health associations in children internationally, and the first such study in the Nordic countries to examine the short-term associations between climatic exposures and hospitalisation risk for children. We found that daily mean temperature and intraday temperature variability were each associated with all-cause hospitalisation, with higher risks at hot temperature extremes and at both low and high levels of within-day temperature variability. Relative humidity showed no association, whereas higher precipitation was associated with increased hospitalisation risk, although estimates became statistically weaker and more imprecise at the highest rainfall levels. The study has several important strengths: it examines different climatic exposures within a single analytical framework; it assesses heterogeneity by age, sex, socioeconomic indicators (parental education and household income), region, calendar period, and parental medical history, showing that risk was highest among younger children and in East Sweden; it evaluates lag-specific and cause-specific associations, showing that heat-related risk was concentrated within the first week of exposure while cause-specific estimates were less precise; and it uses individual-level adjustment for time-invariant characteristics through a within-person case time-series design, controlling for time-invariant individual characteristics and therefore strengthening causal interpretation. Implications of all the available evidenceThe chief implication of this study for public policy is that paediatric hospitalisation risk rises in the days following temperature extremes and periods of high intraday temperature variability, with the largest effects among younger school-age children (6-13 years) and in East Sweden. This supports practical measures such as ensuring reliable access to hydration and shifting the timing of outdoor activity to cooler parts of the day, and, at the healthcare-system level, regionally targeted paediatric surge planning; for example, aligning staffing and emergency capacity with forecasted periods of extreme or highly variable temperature. The chief implication for scientific understanding is that within-day temperature variability represents a distinct dimension of climate-related risk not captured by mean or maximum temperature alone, suggesting heat-health frameworks and early-warning systems built on mean temperature capture only part of the risk. The U-shaped association, with increased risk under both very stable and highly variable conditions, indicates that temperature variability carries information beyond mean thermal load and warrants further investigation. Future research should test whether incorporating variability-metrics improves prediction of paediatric admissions and whether these patterns generalise beyond high-latitude settings.

papers.title: Cumulative Vulnerability and Modern Contraceptive Use in Nigeria: A Latent Class Analysis of the 2018 and 2024 Demographic and Health Surveys
papers.abstract: Modern contraceptive use in Nigeria remains low and unequally distributed. Existing research has extensively examined socioeconomic and demographic determinants, but less is known about how multiple dimensions of disadvantage coexist and relate to contraceptive use. This study identified distinct profiles of cumulative vulnerability among Nigerian women, examined inequalities in modern contraceptive use across these profiles, and assessed changes between 2018 and 2024. We analyzed pooled cross-sectional data from the 2018 and 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Surveys, comprising 80,871 women aged 15-49 years. Latent class analysis was used to identify vulnerability profiles based on six indicators of socioeconomic, informational and empowerment-related disadvantage. Survey-weighted and multilevel logistic regression models were used to examine associations between vulnerability profiles and modern contraceptive use, including differences by survey year. Average marginal effects and adjusted predicted probabilities were estimated. Five vulnerability profiles were identified. The extreme vulnerability profile, characterized by predominantly rural residence, limited education, minimal internet and media access, and low decision-making autonomy, was the largest, accounting for 39.2% of women. Its prevalence increased from 38.3% in 2018 to 40.1% in 2024, while the proportion of women in the most advantaged profile increased from 10.4% to 15.7%. Compared with women in the most advantaged profile, those in the extreme vulnerability profile had a 30.9-percentage-point lower adjusted probability of modern contraceptive use (95% confidence interval: -32.8 to -29.0). This difference was 26.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval: -28.4 to -24.7) after accounting for variation between survey clusters. Adjusted contraceptive use increased across all profiles between 2018 and 2024, but substantial inequalities persisted. Evidence of a differential change for the extreme vulnerability profile was present in the survey-weighted model but not in the multilevel model. Modern contraceptive use in Nigeria is strongly associated with cumulative vulnerability. Despite improvements between 2018 and 2024, substantial inequalities persisted across vulnerability profiles. These findings underscore the importance of addressing overlapping socioeconomic, informational and empowerment-related barriers and monitoring contraceptive-use inequalities across population groups.

papers.title: Stroke Mortality During the War in Ukraine
papers.abstract: BackgroundMounting evidence shows war directly and indirectly harms civilian health. As the largest conflict since World War II, the war in Ukraine severely impacts civilian survival. Stroke--a leading cause of death in Ukraine--represents a key population-level vulnerability to full-scale war. We assessed the wars impact on population-level stroke mortality. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study evaluated patients diagnosed with hemorrhagic or ischemic stroke admitted to Ukrainian civilian hospitals from April 1, 2020, through December 31, 2024. Using data from the Ukrainian nationwide electronic health record system, we compared pre-war and post-war stroke mortality. We used multivariate proportional hazards regression with propensity matching to test if in-hospital mortality increased. Excess deaths were estimated by multiplying the pre-post mortality rate difference by the post-period population in person-days. ResultsAmong 577,501 total individuals, we found that the crude in-hospital stroke mortality rate increased by 117 (95% CI: 94.2-139.9) per 100,000 person-days in the post-war period. In propensity-matched analyses, the mortality risk was 5% (HR=1.05; 95% CI: 1.03-1.06; p<0.001) higher in the post-war period. Mortality risk varied by age, sex, admission type and stroke type. Patients with hemorrhagic stroke had 179% (HR=2.79; 95% CI: 2.75-2.83; p<0.001) higher risk of death compared to ischemic stroke patients. ConclusionIn the first study to assess stroke mortality at the population level in Ukraine after the start of the full-scale war, we found that in-hospital mortality increased in the post-war period with an estimated 3,944 excess stroke deaths.

papers.title: Targeted Free Swimming for Women, Girls, and Older Adults in Tower Hamlets: A RE-AIM Evaluation Study Protocol
papers.abstract: BackgroundResidents of the London Borough of Tower Hamlets experience higher levels of inactivity than national averages, with particularly low participation among women, girls, older adults, and people living in deprived communities. In response, Tower Hamlets launched a targeted free-swimming programme in July 2024, providing free swimming sessions, lessons, coaching clinics, and planned childcare support across four leisure centres. The programme aims to reduce barriers to physical activity, increase participation among underserved groups, and promote health equity. This evaluation seeks to assess the programmes reach, implementation, acceptability, effectiveness, and sustainability. MethodsA mixed-methods evaluation guided by the RE-AIM framework will assess the reach, implementation, acceptability, and effectiveness of the Tower Hamlets free-swimming programme. Quantitative analysis of routine registration and attendance data will examine participant characteristics, programme uptake, and engagement patterns. Qualitative interviews and focus groups with programme users, non-users, and delivery staff will explore experiences, barriers, facilitators, and perceived impacts. Quantitative and qualitative findings will be triangulated to provide a comprehensive understanding of programme delivery and outcomes. Expected OutcomeThe evaluation is expected to generate evidence on the extent to which the programme engages priority populations, including women, girls, and older men. It is anticipated that the study will identify factors influencing programme uptake and sustained engagement, including cultural appropriateness, accessibility, and implementation processes. The evaluation will also provide insights into perceived impacts on physical activity, wellbeing, social connectedness, swimming confidence, and health inequalities. Furthermore, the study is expected to identify the programme components most valued by participants, including free access, women-only sessions, swimming lessons, coaching opportunities, and childcare provision. Implication policy and practiceThe findings will provide actionable evidence to support local authority decision-making regarding the refinement, continuation, and potential expansion of the free-swimming programme. The study will contribute to the evidence base on place-based physical activity interventions designed to address health inequalities in diverse urban populations. For policymakers, the evaluation will offer insights into how subsidised leisure services can improve access to physical activity, enhance community wellbeing, and promote equitable participation among underserved groups.

papers.title: Evaluating ReFresh, a Web-Based Alternative to Suspension for Adolescent E-cigarette Use
papers.abstract: Electronic cigarettes are the most commonly used tobacco product among U.S. adolescents. Schools most often respond to student e-cigarette use with exclusionary discipline such as suspension, which removes students from school and does not address potential underlying nicotine dependence. Web-based alternatives to suspension offer a way to keep students in school while providing cessation-focused support, but evidence on their effects is limited. This study examined changes in e-cigarette-related attitudes and motivation among adolescents who completed ReFresh, a self-paced, web-based alternative-to-suspension program completed in approximately 3 hours. Using a single-group pre-post design, we analyzed data from 173 middle and high school students (grades 6 to 12; mean age 15.0) referred after being caught using e-cigarettes on school grounds across 24 delivery sites (e.g., schools, afterschool programs, and health centers). The program comprises five interactive online lessons grounded in the 5 As clinical framework (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange), motivational interviewing, and cognitive and behavioral skills training. Changes were analyzed with non-parametric tests. After completing ReFresh, participants reported greater motivation to quit ({chi}2 (6) = 22.79,OR = 3.80, 95% CI [2.2,8.8], p < .001) and rated quitting as more important (V = 3037.50,95% CI [1.00, 2.00], p < .001, r = 0.2). They also viewed e-cigarette use as more harmful and more risky (V = 8137.00, 95% CI [0.50, 0.63, p < .001, r = 0.62; V = 7734.50, 95% CI [0.50,0.80), p < .001, r = 0.65)), with the largest shifts in perceived harm relative to cigarettes and perceived risk of mental health problems. Most students reported comfort and confidence seeking help for e-cigarette use or mental health concerns, ranging from 71.10% of students agreeing they felt "More confident asking a trusted adult for help at school" to 80.50% of students agreeing they felt "More confident encouraging a peer to seek help". This study suggests that a brief, web-based alternative to suspension may shift the attitudes and motivation that precede quitting while keeping students in school, offering schools a non-exclusionary way to respond to e-cigarette use. Controlled studies measuring actual e-cigarette behavior are needed to confirm whether these programs reduce use.

papers.title: Identifying Message "Recipes" for High Perceived Effectiveness: Cognitive, Social, and Emotional Profiles of Vaping Public Education Messages Among Young Adults Who Vape
papers.abstract: IntroductionVaping public education campaigns are a central prevention strategy for young adults (YAs), but message effectiveness varies widely and formative testing typically evaluates one message attribute at a time. This study examined how four perceptual dimensions--cognitive engagement, social relevance, emotional arousal, and emotional valence--relate to perceived message effectiveness (PME), and whether multiple combinations of these dimensions correspond to similarly high PME. MethodsIn a cross-sectional online message-testing study conducted from March to April 2025, 540 U.S. YAs who vape each evaluated 15 messages randomly sampled from a corpus of 229 text-image vaping public education messages, yielding 8,100 message evaluations. Cross-classified multilevel models estimated associations between each perceptual dimension and PME. An Explainable Boosting Machine probed nonlinear associations, and k-means clustering of high-predicted-PME perceptual configurations identified distinct profiles. Analyses were conducted in 2026. ResultsCognitive engagement (b = 0.20, 95% CI [0.18, 0.22]) and social relevance (b = 0.15, 95% CI [0.13, 0.17]) showed the strongest associations with PME, followed by emotional arousal (b = 0.06, 95% CI [0.04, 0.08]); emotional valence showed no linear association (b = 0.00, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.02]). The Explainable Boosting Machine revealed a U-shaped valence pattern, with higher predicted PME at both the negative and positive ends of the scale. Clustering yielded five distinct perceptual profiles with similarly high predicted PME (4.10-4.25). ConclusionsMultiple perceptual configurations correspond to similarly high PME, supporting a configurational approach to formative message testing rather than a single optimal message formula.

papers.title: Social Inequities in Healthcare Access Among U.S. Children With ADHD, Autism, and Co-occurring ADHD and Autism: Evidence From the 2023 to 2024 National Survey of Children's Health
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo compare healthcare access among U.S. children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) only, autism only, and co-occurring ADHD-autism, and to identify social inequities associated with unmet care using recent nationally representative data. MethodsWe analyzed combined 2023 to 2024 National Survey of Childrens Health data for 13,576 children aged 3 to 17 years with current ADHD and/or autism. We examined six healthcare-access outcomes: forgone healthcare, unmet mental health care, no medical home, coverage gap/inadequate insurance, unmet specialist care, and unmet care coordination. Survey-weighted modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We combined six multiply imputed poverty measures using Rubins rules. Sensitivity models additionally adjusted for functional difficulty. ResultsCompared with ADHD only, co-occurring ADHD-autism was associated with higher prevalence of forgone healthcare (aPR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.38-2.16), no medical home (1.11; 1.02- 1.20), inadequate or discontinuous insurance (1.14; 1.03-1.28), unmet specialist care (1.49; 1.14-1.94), and unmet care coordination (1.15; 1.04-1.28). Autism only was associated with unmet mental health care (1.49; 1.13-1.97) and care coordination (1.13; 1.02-1.25). Food insufficiency, housing instability, and non-supportive neighborhood conditions were consistently associated with poorer access. After functional difficulty adjustment, associations remained for co-occurring ADHD-autism with forgone and specialist care and for autism only with unmet mental health care. ConclusionsHealthcare access inequities differed by neurodevelopmental diagnostic group and social context. Pediatric systems should strengthen care coordination, specialty and mental health access, insurance continuity, family navigation, and responses to food and housing hardship.
